item.title: BasicsByHand: Logarithms
item.description:
Premise

While reading a book on the history of eee and why it appears everywhere, the author focuses a little on how Napier first developed logarithms. While the book clarifies that Napierian logarithms are different from the definitions we use today, and demonstrates how they were calculated, it occured to me that I had no idea how to derive their values by hand.

Searching online had limited results, and it took me quite some time to find a version that described a simple method that didn’t rely on calculus (something that wasn’t developed fully when logarithms were first calculated).
item.content:encoded:
Premise

While reading a book on the history of eee and why it appears everywhere, the author focuses a little on how Napier first developed logarithms. While the book clarifies that Napierian logarithms are different from the definitions we use today, and demonstrates how they were calculated, it occured to me that I had no idea how to derive their values by hand.

Searching online had limited results, and it took me quite some time to find a version that described a simple method that didn’t rely on calculus (something that wasn’t developed fully when logarithms were first calculated).

I write this down almost entirely from that source, primarily as a means to make one more source available on the internet, and for my own curiosity.

Prerequisites

You need to know very little to read this article.

However, if you truly wish to do it quite literally by hand, you will also need to know how to calculate square roots by hand. I went down this (small) rabbit hole myself while doing this research, and have written down how (again, no calculus involved).

Logarithms and key properties

My “first principles” knowledge on Logarithms was a little rusty. I hope this helps you the same way it did me. However, if you remember your logarithms well, you should skip this section.

What is a logarithm?

The logarithm of a number yyy is defined for a base bbb as the value xxx that satisfies the equation:

y=bxy=b^xy=bx

It is more popularly written as:

log⁡by=x\log_b y=xlogb​y=x

By definition, therefore,

log⁡bbx=x\log_b b^x = xlogb​bx=x

and conversely

blog⁡bx=xb^{\log_bx}=xblogb​x=x

The converse is tricky, but becomes easier if you say log⁡bx=t\log_b x=tlogb​x=t, which implies that bt=xb^t=xbt=x, which is exactly what blog⁡bxb^{\log_b x}blogb​x becomes.

Restrictions on bbb and yyy

It is important to note here that log⁡by\log_b ylogb​y is defined only for y>0y>0y>0 and b>0b>0b>0 and b≠1b \ne 1b=1. These restrictions are necessary for the reasons laid out below:

  1. If b<0b < 0b<0, then bxb^xbx is not always defined (for example, (−2)0.5(-2)^{0.5}(−2)0.5 is not real)
  2. If b=0b = 0b=0, 0x0^x0x is 0 for positive xxx and undefined for x≤0x \leq 0x≤0. It’s not invertible.
  3. If b=1b = 1b=1, 1x=11^x = 11x=1 for all xxx, which doesn’t give a useful log⁡\loglog function.
  4. If y<0y<0y<0 for valid bbb, then no real xxx can satisfy bx>0b^x>0bx>0.
  5. If y=0y=0y=0 for valid bbb, then no real xxx can satisfy bx=0b^x=0bx=0.

Properties of logarithms

Sum of logs to the same base

A very basic property of exponents is that:

bu⋯bv=b⋯b…⋯b⏟(u times)⋯b⋯b…⋯b⏟(v times)=bu+v \begin{aligned} b^u\cdots b^v &= \underbrace{b\cdots b\ldots\cdots b}_\text{(u times)}\cdots \underbrace{b\cdots b\ldots\cdots b}_\text{(v times)}\\ &=b^{u+v} \end{aligned} bu⋯bv​=(u times)b⋯b…⋯b​​⋯(v times)b⋯b…⋯b​​=bu+v​

To extend this to logarithms, define u=log⁡bxu=\log_b xu=logb​x and v=log⁡byv=\log_b yv=logb​y:

bu+v=bu⋯bvblog⁡bx+log⁡by=blog⁡bx⋯blog⁡byblog⁡bx+log⁡by=xyblog⁡bx+log⁡by=blog⁡b(xy)log⁡bx+log⁡by=log⁡b(xy) \begin{aligned} b^{u+v} &= b^u\cdots b^v\\ b^{\log_b x+\log_b y}&=b^{\log_b x}\cdots b^{\log_b y}\\ b^{\log_b x+\log_b y}&=xy\\ b^{\log_b x+\log_b y}&=b^{\log_b{(xy)}}\\ \log_bx+\log_by&=\log_b(xy) \end{aligned} bu+vblogb​x+logb​yblogb​x+logb​yblogb​x+logb​ylogb​x+logb​y​=bu⋯bv=blogb​x⋯blogb​y=xy=blogb​(xy)=logb​(xy)​

It is important that all logs are to the same base bbb.

Logs raised to an arbitrary exponent

This follows directly from sum of logs:

log⁡bxa=log⁡b(x⋯x⋯…⋯x⏟a cdots)=log⁡bx+log⁡bx+…log⁡bx⏟a times=alog⁡bx \begin{aligned} \log_bx^a&=\log_b(\underbrace{x\cdots x\cdots\ldots\cdots x}_{\text{a cdots}})\\ &=\underbrace{\log_bx+\log_b x+\ldots\log_bx}_{\text{a times}}\\ &=a\log_bx \end{aligned} logb​xa​=logb​(a cdotsx⋯x⋯…⋯x​​)=a timeslogb​x+logb​x+…logb​x​​=alogb​x​

Or, when aaa isn’t positive or a whole number, we use the fact that:

(bx)a=bxa=bax (b^x)^a=b^{xa}=b^{ax} (bx)a=bxa=bax

which can be written as:

blog⁡b(ya)=ya=(y)a=(blog⁡by)a=balog⁡by⇒log⁡b(ya)=alog⁡by \begin{aligned} b^{\log_b(y^a)}&=y^a=(y)^a\\ &=(b^{\log_b y})^a\\ &=b^{a\log_b y}\\ \Rightarrow\log_b(y^a)&=a\log_b y \end{aligned} blogb​(ya)⇒logb​(ya)​=ya=(y)a=(blogb​y)a=balogb​y=alogb​y​

Difference of logs

Following the first two properties:

log⁡bx−log⁡by=log⁡bx+(−1)log⁡by=log⁡bx+log⁡by−1=log⁡bx+log⁡b1y=log⁡bxy \begin{aligned} \log_bx-\log_by&=\log_bx+(-1)\log_by\\ &=\log_bx+\log_by^{-1}\\ &=\log_bx+\log_b\frac{1}{y}\\ &=\log_b\frac{x}{y} \end{aligned} logb​x−logb​y​=logb​x+(−1)logb​y=logb​x+logb​y−1=logb​x+logb​y1​=logb​yx​​

Changing of base

This is an important one. We need to write:

log⁡xy \log_xy logx​y

in the form of just logs to a common base bbb. We can write:

xlog⁡bylog⁡bx=(blog⁡bx)log⁡bylog⁡bx=blog⁡bx⋯log⁡bylog⁡bx=blog⁡by=y=xlog⁡xy⇒log⁡bylog⁡bx=log⁡xy \begin{aligned} x^\frac{\log_by}{\log_bx}&=(b^{\log_bx})^\frac{\log_by}{\log_bx}\\ &=b^{\frac{\log_bx\cdots\log_by}{\log_bx}}\\ &=b^{\log_by}\\ &=y\\ &=x^{\log_xy}\\ \Rightarrow \dfrac{\log_by}{\log_bx}&=\log_xy \end{aligned} xlogb​xlogb​y​⇒logb​xlogb​y​​=(blogb​x)logb​xlogb​y​=blogb​xlogb​x⋯logb​y​=blogb​y=y=xlogx​y=logx​y​

The Euler Method

Let’s say that we want to calculate log⁡7155\log_7 155log7​155. Euler’s method involved first changing the base:

log⁡7155=log⁡10155log⁡107 \log_7 155=\dfrac{\log_{10} 155}{\log_{10} 7} log7​155=log10​7log10​155​

and then using the identity:

log⁡(x⋅y)=log⁡(xy)2=log⁡x+log⁡y2 \log(\sqrt{x\cdot y})=\dfrac{\log(xy)}{2}=\dfrac{\log x+\log y}{2} log(x⋅y​)=2log(xy)​=2logx+logy​

Let’s see how. From herewith, if only log⁡\loglog is used, assume that it means log⁡10\log_{10}log10​. This will simplify a lot of the visual noise.

Simplifying log calculations

We can first start by writing:

log⁡155=log⁡(100⋅1.55)=2+log⁡1.55 \log155=\log(100\cdot1.55)=2+\log1.55 log155=log(100⋅1.55)=2+log1.55

Calculating log⁡1.55\log1.55log1.55

Iteration 1

We know that from the identity above:

log⁡(1⋅10)=log⁡1+log⁡102=12=0.5 \log(\sqrt{1\cdot10}) = \dfrac{\log1 +\log10}{2}=\dfrac{1}{2}=0.5 log(1⋅10​)=2log1+log10​=21​=0.5

In other words,

log⁡10=0.5 \log{\sqrt{10}} = 0.5 log10​=0.5

We know (or can calculate by hand) that 10≈3.16228\sqrt{10}\approx3.1622810​≈3.16228. You can hopefully now see where this is going.

Iteration 2

Where does 1.551.551.55 lie? Between 111 and 10\sqrt{10}10​, or between 111 and 3.162283.162283.16228. Let’s now calculate:

log⁡1⋅3.16228=log⁡1+log⁡3.162282=0+0.52=0.25 \log{\sqrt{1\cdot3.16228}}=\dfrac{\log1+\log3.16228}{2}=\dfrac{0+0.5}{2}=0.25 log1⋅3.16228​=2log1+log3.16228​=20+0.5​=0.25

Thus, 1⋅3.16228\sqrt{1\cdot3.16228}1⋅3.16228​ is 3.16228=1.77828\sqrt{3.16228}=1.778283.16228​=1.77828.

Iteration 3

Once again, we make more progress by finding the square root of 1.778281.778281.77828, because 1.551.551.55 lies between 111 and 1.778281.778281.77828. Therefore,

log⁡1⋅1.77828=log⁡1+log⁡1.778282=0.125 \log{\sqrt{1\cdot1.77828}}=\dfrac{\log1+\log{1.77828}}{2}=0.125 log1⋅1.77828​=2log1+log1.77828​=0.125

1.77828≈1.33521\sqrt{1.77828}\approx1.335211.77828​≈1.33521. We’re getting rather close.

Iteration 4

We have a small change here. 1.551.551.55 now lies between 1.335211.335211.33521 and 1.778281.778281.77828. This means that the new value we need to find is:

log⁡1.33521⋅1.77828=log⁡1.33521+log⁡1.778282=0.125+0.252=0.1875 \begin{aligned} \log{\sqrt{1.33521\cdot1.77828}}&=\dfrac{\log{1.33521}+\log{1.77828}}{2}\\ &=\dfrac{0.125+0.25}{2}\\ &=0.1875 \end{aligned} log1.33521⋅1.77828​​=2log1.33521+log1.77828​=20.125+0.25​=0.1875​

Also, 1.33521⋅1.77828=1.54090\sqrt{1.33521\cdot1.77828}=1.540901.33521⋅1.77828​=1.54090

Further iterations

The next step would be to determine if 1.540901.540901.54090 is sufficiently close to 1.551.551.55 for us to approximate that log⁡1.54090≈log⁡1.55\log 1.54090\approx\log 1.55log1.54090≈log1.55, or we need to proceed further.

Of course, we can continue to refine the values until we’re sufficiently satisfied of our accuracy. What does a calculator tell us about log⁡1.55\log 1.55log1.55?

1>>> from math import log
2>>> log(1.55, 10)
30.1903316981702915

So we were off by around… 0.00280.00280.0028, which isn’t bad at all, considering we did only around 4 iterations (and many more iterations for calculating the square root).

Back to the Euler method

We find that log⁡10155=2+0.1875\log_{10}155=2+0.1875log10​155=2+0.1875. We calculate log⁡107\log_{10}7log10​7 the same way, which should come to 0.8450.8450.845 (according to my calculator), so

log⁡7155≈2.18750.845=2.5 \log_7 155\approx\dfrac{2.1875}{0.845}=2.5 log7​155≈0.8452.1875​=2.5

and calculators give us:

1>>> from math import log
2>>> log(155, 7)
32.591

Clearly, while this is close to the 2.52.52.5 we got, it’s not quite correct - we’re off by 0.0910.0910.091, an order of magnitude more. If we’d used the true value, 0.19030.19030.1903, then we would have got:

log⁡7155≈2.19030.845≈2.592 \log_7 155\approx\dfrac{2.1903}{0.845}\approx2.592 log7​155≈0.8452.1903​≈2.592

Which is much closer to the true value. We find that approximating the true value of the log to a much larger number of decimal points is crucial to get the correct value.

Takeaway

A key takeaway for a programmer would be that Euler managed to implement binary search to efficiently (especially in terms of human effort) find the logarithm of a number

References

The primary reference for the material in this article is Bureau42. While the link works, it looks like the material that this used to point to doesn’t anymore. Some searching led me to a backup hosted on GitHub and another Hackernews linked source.

item.title: BasicsByHand: Square Roots
item.description:
Premise

Long ago in middle school (or even earlier), along with the concept of what a square root is, I was also taught a method to calculate them by hand. This method did not involve Taylor series expansions, nor was it the popular numeric Newton-Raphson method - we didn’t have a lick of knowledge of Calculus to use them anyway.

It worked, and nobody ever quite taught why it worked. Given that I’m an adult now and free to do adult things, I wanted to cross this off my (admittedly non-existent) list as a part of something else I was trying to understand.
item.content:encoded:
Premise

Long ago in middle school (or even earlier), along with the concept of what a square root is, I was also taught a method to calculate them by hand. This method did not involve Taylor series expansions, nor was it the popular numeric Newton-Raphson method - we didn’t have a lick of knowledge of Calculus to use them anyway.

It worked, and nobody ever quite taught why it worked. Given that I’m an adult now and free to do adult things, I wanted to cross this off my (admittedly non-existent) list as a part of something else I was trying to understand.

What method?

This is for my readers who may not be familiar with this method, or just need a refresher. Suppose you need to calculate the square root of 78129.329 while you’re stuck on an island. Maybe your captor is a math fanatic. This is how you would go about it.

Start with grouping the digits in pairs - starting from the decimal point, moving on either side of it:

       ┌─────────────────
       │  7,81,29.32,9

Now, we begin a method that suspiciously looks a lot like long-form division. Find the largest number whose square is equal to, or less than the left-most group.

           2
        ┌─────────────────
      2 │  7,81,29.32,9

Then, you subtract its square from the digit:

           2
        ┌─────────────────
      2 │  7,81,29.32,9
        │ -4
        │─────────────────
        │  3

and multiply the number at the top with 2 (how arbitrary! or is it…?) and call it the new divisor you’re going to work with. The next task is to find a value for a digit xxx such that x×(40+x)x \times (40+x)x×(40+x) is less than or equal to 381381381:

           2  x
        ┌─────────────────
      2 │  7,81,29.32,9
        │ -4
        │─────────────────
     4x │  3,81

This will require some manual multiplication (since we’re doing this by hand!). Looks like 777 meets this requirement (as 48×8=38448 \times 8 = 38448×8=384). Apply the same subtraction:

           2  7
        ┌─────────────────
      2 │  7,81,29.32,9
        │ -4
        │─────────────────
     47 │  3,81
        │ -3,29
        │─────────────────
        │   52

and repeat the process once more. We need to first multiply 272727 by 222, which gives us 545454. Similarly, x×(540+x)x \times (540+x)x×(540+x) should then be less than or equal to 52,2952,2952,29:

           2  7  x
        ┌─────────────────
      2 │  7,81,29.32,9
        │ -4
        │─────────────────
     47 │  3,81
        │ -3,29
        │─────────────────
    54x │    52,29

I’ll forgive you if you use the calculator here! I’ll skip a step here (we end up at 999 as 549×9=49,41<52,29549\times 9=49,41<52,29549×9=49,41<52,29) to show that we need to now find xxx such that x×(5580+x)x \times (5580 + x)x×(5580+x) is less than or equal to 2,88,322,88,322,88,32:

           2  7  9. x
        ┌─────────────────
      2 │  7,81,29.32,9
        │ -4
        │─────────────────
     47 │  3,81
        │ -3,29
        │─────────────────
    549 │    52,29
        │   -49,41
        │─────────────────
   558x │     2,88,32

We settle on 5. Note here that the next number is 2795×22795\times22795×2, not 279.5×2279.5\times2279.5×2, a small subtlety here. The next xxx is going to be 111:

           2  7  9. 5 x
        ┌─────────────────
      2 │  7,81,29.32,9
        │ -4
        │─────────────────
     47 │  3,81
        │ -3,29
        │─────────────────
    549 │    52,29
        │   -49,41
        │─────────────────
   5585 │     2,88,32     
        │    -2,79,25
        │─────────────────
  5590x │        9,07,90

and we get:

           2  7  9. 5 1
        ┌─────────────────
      2 │  7,81,29.32,9
        │ -4
        │─────────────────
     47 │  3,81
        │ -3,29
        │─────────────────
    549 │    52,29
        │   -49,41
        │─────────────────
   5585 │     2,88,32     
        │    -2,79,25
        │─────────────────
  55901 │        9,07,90
        │      - 5,59,01
        │─────────────────
        │        3,48,89

We could stop here, or go on further. I elect to stop here, and verify my result. Let’s go to trusty Python:

1>>> from math import sqrt
2>>> print(sqrt(7_81_29.32_9))
3279.51624103082094

Excellent, so we were right!

But… why? How did we get it right?

Building the Intuition

Getting our foot in the door

Let’s start with our previous example.

7,81,29.32,9 7,81,29.32,9 7,81,29.32,9

Note that commas intentionally retained every two digits instead of the usual three.

Why are commands retained every two digits?

This is because squares of numbers have, up to twice the number of digits of the original number. Anecdotally, consider 9992999^29992. It will be less than 100021000^210002, which is 1,000,0001,000,0001,000,000 and has 7 digits (and 7 is less than 4, the number of digits that 100010001000) has.

On the other hand, smaller numbers like 444 go to 161616 (111 digit to 222 digits). 111 to 333 remain at 111 digit (1, 4, 9).

Remember that we usually also write our numbers in base 101010. Since any power of 101010 is easy to calculate, this makes the estimate of our first digit rather easy. Let’s start by finding the closest square of 101010 that is less than or equal to 7,81,29.3297,81,29.3297,81,29.329.

1,00,00≤7,81,29.329≤10,00,00⇒104≤7,81,29.32,9≤105⇒(102)2≤7,81,29.32,9≤105 \begin{array}{lrll} &1,00,00 &\leq 7,81,29.329 &\leq 10,00,00\\ \Rightarrow &10^4 &\leq 7,81,29.32,9 &\leq 10^5\\ \Rightarrow &(10^2)^2 &\leq 7,81,29.32,9 &\leq 10^5\\ \end{array} ⇒⇒​1,00,00104(102)2​≤7,81,29.329≤7,81,29.32,9≤7,81,29.32,9​≤10,00,00≤105≤105​

Why did we write this as (102)2(10^2)^2(102)2? This tells us that our desired square root is greater than 100100100. What’s the closest multiple of hundred that is less than or equal to 7,81,29.32,97,81,29.32,97,81,29.32,9? It’s 200, because

2002=4,00,00<7,81,29.32,93002=9,00,00>7,81,29.32,9 \begin{array}{rlr} 200^2 &= 4,00,00 &< 7,81,29.32,9\\ 300^2 &= 9,00,00 &> 7,81,29.32,9 \end{array} 20023002​=4,00,00=9,00,00​<7,81,29.32,9>7,81,29.32,9​

In other words,

2002≤7,81,29.32,9≤3002 \begin{array}{lrll} &200^2 &\leq 7,81,29.32,9 &\leq 300^2\\ \end{array} ​2002​≤7,81,29.32,9​≤3002​

When we calculated that 200200200 was the closest multiple of 100100100 that was less than or equal to 7,81,29.32,97,81,29.32,97,81,29.32,9, we were calculating the first digit of the square root.

We continue by applying a common formula…

…which is derived below to minimize cognitive load, in case it’s been a long time since you’ve touched algebra.

(a+x)2=(a+x)(a+x)=a(a+x)+x(a+x)=a2+ax+xa+x2=a2+2ax+x2 \begin{aligned} (a+x)^2 &=(a+x)(a+x)\\ &=a(a+x) + x(a+x)\\ &=a^2 + ax + xa + x^2\\ &=a^2+2ax+x^2 \end{aligned} (a+x)2​=(a+x)(a+x)=a(a+x)+x(a+x)=a2+ax+xa+x2=a2+2ax+x2​

Connecting the dots

Let’s consider the next digit. Because the true root lies between 200200200 and 300300300, we can say that the next digit of the root will be the closest multiple of 101010 that is greater than 200200200 and whose square is less than 7,81,29.32,97,81,29.32,97,81,29.32,9.

That means we’re trying to find a single digit xxx that meets the criteria:

(200+10x)2≤7,81,29.32,9⇒2002+2⋅200⋅10x+100x2≤7,81,29.32,9⇒2002+100⋅(40+x)x≤7,81,29.32,9⇒100⋅(40+x)x≤3,81,29.32,9⇒(40+x)x≤3,81.29,32,9 \begin{array}{rll} &(200+10x)^2 &\leq 7,81,29.32,9\\ \Rightarrow &200^2 + 2\cdot200\cdot10x + 100x^2 &\leq 7,81,29.32,9\\ \Rightarrow &200^2 + 100\cdot\boldsymbol{(40+x)x} &\leq 7,81,29.32,9\\ \Rightarrow &100\cdot\boldsymbol{(40+x)x} &\leq 3,81,29.32,9\\ \Rightarrow &\boldsymbol{(40+x)x} &\leq \boldsymbol{3,81}.29,32,9 \end{array} ⇒⇒⇒⇒​(200+10x)22002+2⋅200⋅10x+100x22002+100⋅(40+x)x100⋅(40+x)x(40+x)x​≤7,81,29.32,9≤7,81,29.32,9≤7,81,29.32,9≤3,81,29.32,9≤3,81.29,32,9​

Look closely at the bolded parts of the last equation:

(40+x)x≤3,81 \boldsymbol{(40+x)x} \leq \boldsymbol{3,81} (40+x)x≤3,81

This is exactly what we did here:

           2  x
        ┌─────────────────
      2 │  7,81,29.32,9
        │ -4
        │─────────────────
     4x │  3,81

The single digit xxx that satisfies this equation is 777, as we had obtained earlier.

One more step for clearer understanding

Let’s do one more round to inscribe the logic in our heads:

We know that 270270270 is the next best approximation of the root of 7,81,29.3297,81,29.3297,81,29.329. We also know that to get the next digit, we need the closest multiple of 111 that is between 270270270 and 280280280 whose square is less than 7,81,29.32,97,81,29.32,97,81,29.32,9.

Once again, in trying to find the single digit xxx, the expressions become (note that in this iteration, xxx is just xxx, not 10x10x10x, because it’s a multiple of 111, not 101010):

(270+x)2≤7,81,29.32,9⇒2702+2⋅270⋅x+x2≤7,81,29.32,9⇒2702+(540+x)x≤7,81,29.32,9⇒(540+x)x≤52,29.32,9⇒(540+x)x≤52,29.32,9 \begin{array}{rll} &(270+x)^2 &\leq 7,81,29.32,9\\ \Rightarrow &270^2 + 2\cdot270\cdot x + x^2 &\leq 7,81,29.32,9\\ \Rightarrow &270^2 + \boldsymbol{(540+x)x} &\leq 7,81,29.32,9\\ \Rightarrow &\boldsymbol{(540+x)x} &\leq 52,29.32,9\\ \Rightarrow &\boldsymbol{(540+x)x} &\leq \boldsymbol{52,29}.32,9 \end{array} ⇒⇒⇒⇒​(270+x)22702+2⋅270⋅x+x22702+(540+x)x(540+x)x(540+x)x​≤7,81,29.32,9≤7,81,29.32,9≤7,81,29.32,9≤52,29.32,9≤52,29.32,9​

and the bolded parts of the expression are:

(540+x)x≤52,29 \boldsymbol{(540+x)x} \leq \boldsymbol{52,29} (540+x)x≤52,29

once again, matching exactly to:

           2  7  x
        ┌─────────────────
      2 │  7,81,29.32,9
        │ -4
        │─────────────────
     47 │  3,81
        │ -3,29
        │─────────────────
    54x │    52,29

Estimating to more decimal points

You also now understand why this process can continue on till as many decimal points are needed.

The rest of the estimation, however, is, um… left as an exercise to the reader 😬.

Conclusion

I hope you now understand that the so called “long-division” method is just encoding the technique that I laid out above step-by-step, and is not really doing division alone, it’s extending the binomial identity (a+b)2(a+b)^2(a+b)2 and refining it successively every iteration.

You will also notice that as we proceed further in calculating the root, the smaller the error becomes, allowing us to ignore it when we see fit.
